news.title: World Briefing | Americas: Brazil: Runoff For São Paulo

news.abstract: Cambodian Parliament's lower house finally ratifies agreement with United Nations to create international tribunal to try surviving leaders of Communist Khmer Rouge for atrocities during their four-year rule in late 1970's; no timetable is set for trial and some technical and political issues lie ahead, including need to raise estimated $57 million from international donors; none of aging Khmer Rouge leaders have been brought into court; during their reign, as many as one-fourth of Cambodian population died from execution, starvation, overwork and disease; seven major figures are main focus of possible proceedings, but only two are in custody; Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot died in 1998 (M)
news.title: Lawmakers in Cambodia Vote to Try Khmer Rouge

news.abstract: Whenever a Japanese convoy leaves its base here in southern Iraq, the armored vehicles are so spotless that they appear to have just rolled out of a Tokyo car showroom into this crumbling Shiite Muslim town on the Euphrates.     They lack the dents and dirt of other nations' vehicles. Perhaps that is because of the Japanese troops' attention to maintenance or perhaps, as the Iraqis here say, their increasing tendency to stay inside their base with the violence rising outside.
news.title: Japan's Troops Proceed in Iraq Without Shot Fired

news.abstract: Mohamed El Baradei, director of International Atomic Energy Agency, visits Korean peninsula and warns both North and South Korea on nuclear weapons; urges South Korea to maintain control over its program; says he will visit North Korea and urges UN Security Council to have 'smart sanctions' ready to target recalcitrant countries without adding misery to citizens (M)
news.title: Director of U.N. Nuclear Agency, in Seoul, Cautions Both Koreas

news.abstract: A reassessment by the Central Intelligence Agency has cast doubt on a central piece of evidence used by the Bush administration before the invasion of Iraq to draw links between Saddam Hussein's government and Al Qaeda's terrorist network, government officials said Tuesday.    The C.I.A. report, sent to policy makers in August, says it is now not clear whether Mr. Hussein's government harbored members of a group led by the Jordanian terrorist Abu Musab al-Zarqawi, the officials said. The assertion that Iraq provided refuge to Mr. Zarqawi was the primary basis for the administration's prewar assertions connecting Iraq to Al Qaeda.
news.title: A New C.I.A. Report Casts Doubt on a Key Terrorist's Tie to Iraq

news.abstract: Jan Pronk, the United Nations envoy to Sudan, told the Security Council that the government in Khartoum has made no progress on protecting the embattled people of the country's Darfur region or in bringing to justice the leaders of rampaging Arab militias. Among the continuing attacks, he said, were those by army helicopters. He said the priority now was in deploying the promised 4,000-man force from the African Union. John C. Danforth, the United States ambassador to the United Nations, said he was concerned about predictions that the full force might not be in place until the end of the year.   Warren Hoge (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Africa: Sudan: No Progress In Darfur Crisis, U.N. Told

news.abstract: Michael Howard, the leader of Britain's Conservative Party, urged Tories on Tuesday to focus on discontent with Prime Minister Tony Blair's domestic record and his failure to ''tell the truth'' in the months before the war in Iraq as the best strategy for contesting the national elections expected next spring.    In his first address to the annual Conservative Party gathering, Mr. Howard also sought to stem defections to the upstart U.K. Independence Party, which has eroded Conservatives' base by taking a hard line against immigration and membership in the European Union.
news.title: Tory Leader Outlines Domestic Focus for Campaign Against Blair
Appeal hearings openfor 2 former Elf chiefs

news.abstract: Turks react with relief to European Commission's qualified endorsement of their country's bid to start talks for membership to European Union; civic and business leaders acknowledge they face more formidable battle to win hearts and minds of European public; many say they would reserve their celebrations for mid-Dec meeting of EU leaders, who will make decision whether to put Turkey on road to eventual entry (M)
news.title: A Step Closer to Europe, Proud Turks Hold Off Glee

news.abstract: Five neo-Nazis suspected of planning bomb attack on Munich's new Jewish cultural center go on trial; foiled plot, planned for Nov 9, 2003, would have been during cornerstone laying ceremony for center (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Germany: 5 Go On Trial In Plot On Jewish Center

news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Russia: 10 Qaeda Agents Said To Be In Caucasus

news.abstract: King Norodom Sihanouk's decision to give up throne he has held, off and on, for more than half century throws Cambodia into confusion and doubt; although his power is almost entirely symbolic, he has been soul of Cambodia since he was installed by its French colonial rulers in 1941; he is 81 and in poor health; in recent months he has said he feels marginalized as Cambodian politicians struggle to form government after inconclusive election in July 2003 (M)
news.title: Abdication by Cambodia's King Throws His Nation Into Confusion

news.abstract: Nobel Peace Prize is awarded to Dr Wangari Maathai, Kenyan woman who started environmental movement that has planted 30 million trees in Africa; Maathai founded Green Belt Movement in 1977 to organize poor women to fight deforestation and to replenish fuel source; award stretches traditional bounds of prize to include environmental advocacy; Nobel committee calls her 'inspiration for everyone in Africa fighting for sustainable development, democracy and peace'; photo (M)
news.title: Peace Prize Goes to Environmentalist in Kenya

news.title: Names of the Dead

news.abstract: Lt Col Steven L Jordan testified to Army investigators in February that Central Intelligence Agency kept prisoners off books in Iraq to speed their transfer to sites outside Iraq where they would not be protected by Geneva Conventions; says CIA had unwritten agreement with Col Thomas M Pappas, top military intelligence officer at Abu Ghraib prison; others have said that prisoners were kept off books to hide them from Red Cross (M)
news.title: Inmates Were Reportedly Kept Off Books to Speed Transfer

news.abstract: Hardline politicians in Iranian Parliament have forced government to cancel contracts with two Turkish companies, and other companies have been scared off; goal of hardliners is to paralyze government and shut it out of international affairs; Ayatollah Ali Khamenei allowed sale of state-owned banks, but Parliament has blocked sale of $5.95 billion in state assets; Pres Mohammad Khatami's moderate government attracted more foreign investment in two years than Iran has had in previous 20 years; photo (M)
news.title: Conservatives in Iran Battle the Spread of Foreign Investment

news.abstract: Australian Prime Min John Howard of Liberal Party is decisively elected to fourth term; preliminary results show Liberals winning 71 of 150 seats in House of Representatives and coalition partner National Party taking 12 seats; Australia's participation in Iraq war is widely unpopular, but booming economy was key issue (M)
news.title: Australians Re-electHoward as Prime Minister

news.abstract: Afghans turn out to vote in large numbers in their first presidential election; unexpectedly peaceful event is marred by 15 candidates' claim of widespread cheating and fraud and request for new vote; criticism casts shadow on what is otherwise historic success for Afghans who have endured more than two decades of war and turmoil; officials say results could take two to three weeks to be tallied; expected threat to elections from Taliban insurgents generally fails to materialize; throughout country, Afghans line up patiently tocast their votes; Pres Bush, campaigning for his re-election, hails arrival of elections in Afghanistan; problem is encountered with ink placed on each voter's thumb to prevent multiple votes; many voters find they could erase it minutes after voting and, if they had extra card, vote again; UN and Afghan officials briefly consider suspending voting, then decide against it; Pres Hamid Karzai's 15 rivals seize on problem and proclaim election illegitimate; photo; diagrams (L)
news.title: Afghan Poll Is Mostly Calm, but Challengers Cry Foul

news.abstract: Poor intelligence offsets superior American military technology in hunt for Iraqi insurgents; officers maintain optimism, but troops are frustrated; raids may turn up weapons but rarely people; pursuit of fleeing suspects is awkward amid irrigated fields and language difficulties hamper communications with frightened farmers; map; photos (M)
news.title: Scouring Iraq for Enemies, Finding Farmers and Mud

news.abstract: Iraqi and American officials and aides to rebel Shiite cleric Moktada al-Sadr announce agreement to disband Sadr's militia; say his Mahdi Army fighters will hand over their heavy weapons to Iraqi police next week from their stronghold in Sadr City, following weeks of fighting with American forces; Sadr has been greatly weakened since being upstaged by Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sisatani; Iraqi and American officials are cautiously optimistic, noting that Sadr has history of renegging on pledges to disarm; his fighters are intensely loyal to him, but some leaders inside movement doubt they would actually obey order to give up their large weapons; policing agreement would be extremely difficult; under accord, American commanders say they would continue to patrol Sadr City, but would not attack Mahdi Army, except in retaliation; any deal that neutralizes Mahdi Army would allow American military and Iraqi government to turn energies toward insurgency's core, in Sunni Arab lands north and west of Baghdad; photo (M)
news.title: Iraqi Cleric's Militia in Sadr City Promises to Hand Over Arms

news.abstract: Researchers say vaccine against malaria has shown for first time that it can save children from infection or death; vaccine, tested on thousands of children in Mozambique, is hardly perfect: it protected them from catching disease only about 30 percent of time and prevented it from becoming life-threatening only about 58 percent of time; but because malaria kills more than million people a year, 700,000 of them children, even partial protection would be public health victory; disease, caused by parasite carried by mosquitoes, is found in 90 countries, and drug-resistant strains are spreading; director of Malaria Vaccine Initiative, which is underwriting tests on 15 experimental vaccines with money from Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, says that GlaxoSmithKline product tried in Mozambique is now its leading candidate and had proved that concept works; photo of mosquito (L)
news.title: Malaria Vaccine Proves Effective

news.abstract: YASER E. HAMDI, a high school honor student from a privileged Saudi background, was a sophomore in college, majoring in marketing, when he took off for Afghanistan during the summer of 2001.     His father, who spells his name Himdy, says it was just one of those things young men do, to find themselves or to satisfy a yearning for adventure. ''Boys like to try things new,'' Mr. Himdy said. ''He had never traveled outside Saudi Arabia before. He decided to show, 'I am a man.'''
news.title: From Afghanistan to Saudi Arabia, via Guantánamo
Vowing Iraq pullback, Polish leader wins vote

news.abstract: The Department of Defense has identified 1,082 American service members who have died since the start of the Iraq war. It confirmed the deaths of the following Americans yesterday:    BAKER, Ronald W., 34, Specialist, Army National Guard; Cabot, Ark.; 39th Support Battalion.    REGNIER, Jeremy F., 22, Specialist, Army; Littleton, N.H.; First Cavalry Division.
news.title: Names of the Dead

news.abstract: American forces stepped up their pressure on the insurgent-controlled city of Falluja on Friday, unleashing an aerial and artillery bombardment of suspected guerrilla positions and encircling the city with hundreds of marines at checkpoints along its main roads.    Beginning Thursday, American jets began their most intense bombardment of the city yet, dropping 11 satellite- and laser-guided 500-pound bombs on suspected guerrilla safe houses and weapons depots, as 1,600 American marines moved forward under artillery fire to set up the checkpoints, designed to snare insurgents moving out of the city.
news.title: U.S. Intensifying Bombing Attacks on Falluja Sites

news.abstract: Three children, two American soldiers and an Afghan policeman died in two new attacks by people suspected of being Taliban rebels in Afghanistan, Afghan and American officials announced Saturday.     Two American soldiers died and three others were wounded on Thursday when an improvised bomb detonated under their vehicle in Uruzgan Province in southern Afghanistan, the American military officials said.
news.title: 6 Killed in Attacks In 2 Afghan Regions

news.abstract: American military commanders in Iraq are warning civilian leaders in Washington that delays in reconstruction projects caused by red tape are putting the lives of their troops at risk and undermining the military mission in Iraq.     From the junior officer level up through the senior ranks, these officers have outlined obstacles that they say frustrate the rebuilding just as much as the roadside bombs and terrorist attacks that are the more visible threats. They have argued to the new American Embassy in Baghdad and to Congressional delegations visiting Iraq that certain regulations are a dangerous impediment to the military's mission.
news.title: Iraq Commanders Warn That Delays in Civil Projects Undermine Military Mission

news.abstract: The first sign of change is a sign, posted on the brown mud exterior wall of Soheila Helal's house and garden to announce her private courses. When the Taliban controlled this western city, Ms. Helal had to teach in secret. Now she is free to advertise.     Nearly three years ago, days after the Taliban left the city ending almost six years of repressive rule, Ms. Helal was one of a host of women interviewed by The New York Times. They recounted lives cloistered and hopes curtailed through days that blurred to months, then years.
news.title: Free of Taliban's Yoke, 2 Afghan Women Rise Again

news.abstract: Israel and United Nations Relief and Works Agency have had running battle; Israel claims agency's Palestinian workers help Palestinian militants, and that militants have often gained access to UN ambulances, schools and other facilities; agency's director Peter Hansen says Israel has frequently raised false or inflated accusations against it and has consistently hampered aid efforts by imposing stringent travel restrictions against its personnel in West Bank and Gaza Strip; since 2001, Israel has arrested and indicted 17 of agency's workers, accusing them of assisting militants; seven have been convicted by military courts; in incident in Gaza City in May, four Palestinian gunmen climbed into UN ambulance after placing wounded comrade inside; incident was captured by television cameraman, and Israeli military contends Palestinians used ambulance to escape; photo (M)
news.title: Israel Feuds With Agency Set Up to Aid Palestinians

news.abstract: Effort is under way in Europe to train clerics to minister to growing population of Muslims in Europe, in hope of stanching migration of clerics who are beholden to foreign interests and, in some cases, full of hate and capable of terrorist acts; perceived threat is so great that some European governments closely monitor activities and sermons of their Muslim clerics; France has expelled more than dozen Muslim clerics for violations of human rights or public order since 2001; in Italy, Senegalese-born imam was expelled after calling for suicide bombings and declaring 'blood pact' with Osama bin Laden; Britian is charging militant Muslim cleric Abu Hamza al-Masri, supporter of Osama bin Laden, with terrorism offenses, stalling American effort to extradite him to United States; creating army of learned, law-abiding, Europeanized imams will not be easy because in Europe, government involvement in religion can be seen as violation of privacy and human rights; photos; map (M)
news.title: Europe Struggling to Train New Breed of Muslim Clerics

news.abstract: A coalition of health care groups is warning that the sale of cheaper prescription drugs to customers in the United States could lead to drug shortages in Canada. The group, Best Medicines Coalition, is urging the federal government to stop the growing Internet trade in drugs, which are cheaper in Canada because of government price controls. While importing drugs from Canada has been offered as a solution to their high cost in the United States, most notably by Senator John Kerry, many health care experts in Canada say the country cannot support a huge increase in demand. ''They are talking about raiding our medicine cabinet,'' said Louise Binder, a member of the coalition.   Colin Campbell (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Americas: Canada: Call To Stop Export Of Drugs
Spitting incident fuels debate on intolerance

news.abstract: South Africa's Foreign Ministry rejected ''with contempt'' an accusation by Haiti's prime minister, Gérard Latortue, that President Thabo Mbeki had allowed the deposed Haitian president, Jean-Bertrand Aristide, now in exile in South Africa at the Mbeki government's expense, to mount a campaign to destabilize his old homeland. At least 50 people have died in recent violence in Haiti fomented largely by pro-Aristide gangs. Mr. Latortue was quoted Sunday as saying that Mr. Mbeki had ignored international law by giving Mr. Aristide free rein ''to organize violence'' in Haiti from his South African refuge.   Michael Wines (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Americas: Haiti: South Africa Denies Aristide Claims

news.abstract: Edmary Mpagi, who spent 18 years on Uganda's death row before being acquitted of crime, is part of growing movement to eliminate death penalty in Africa; 15 years ago, only Cape Verde Islands did not have death penalty; now 10 countries have outlawed practice and 10 more have abolished its use; proponents of death penalty include religious leaders, particularly Islamic courts, and citizens who fear violent criminal activity; Uganda, which has 417 people on death row, supports harsh penalties, but has not carried out execution since March 2003; Uganda Citizen's Rescue activist Godfrey Ssebuwufu supports abolishing capital punishment; investigates cases of those individuals on death row and seeks to have verdicts overturned; Edmary Mpagi was released as result of Ssebuwufu's diligence to save innocent lives; photo (M)
news.title: Foes of Death Penalty Making Gradual Gains in Africa

news.abstract: United Nations Security Council urges Syria to comply with Sept 2 resolution that all foreign troops pull out of Lebanon; calls for Syria to withdraw 14,000 troops believed to be in place there; Syrian Foreign Minister Farouk al-Sharaa and Lebanese Foreign Ministry hold United Nations has no jurisdiction in bilateral relations between nations (S)
news.title: World Briefing | United Nations: Renewed Call For Syria To Leave Lebanon

news.abstract: The senior law enforcement official in Chechnya announced Friday that the authorities had nearly captured Aslan Maskhadov, one of the best-known leaders of the Chechen resistance, and that Mr. Maskhadov was planning to surrender soon.     The announcement, made by the first deputy prime minister, Ramzan Kadyrov, in Grozny, the Chechen capital, underscored the sense of urgency driving the hunts for senior separatists. It also exposed the tension among the Russian security agencies conducting them.
news.title: Chechen Rebel Leader Is Reported to Be Close to Surrendering

news.abstract: Five years after the United Nations took over the administration of Kosovo, the southern province of Serbia, the residents vote this weekend in an election that may be crucial in determining whether it becomes independent.    The vote for the 120-seat Parliament is the second since NATO troops forced Serbian security forces responsible for widespread atrocities out of the province in June 1999, making Kosovo an international protectorate. Half a decade later, Kosovo remains home to NATO's largest peacekeeping force, and the election has focused the minds of the ethnic Albanian majority, who make up over 90 percent of the 1.8 million people, most of whom are impatient for an end to the international control.
news.title: Still Deeply Divided, Nervous Kosovo Goes to Polls This Weekend
Kosovo election a crucial test for independence

news.abstract: Vladimir Herzog died in military custody nearly 30 years ago in what remains one of the most notorious cases of human rights abuse in Brazil. Now the publication of a pair of photographs said to have been taken in his last hours has reopened that old wound and widened differences between the armed forces and the left-wing government that is now in office here.    The army's attempt, decades after the episode, to justify its treatment of Mr. Herzog and several hundred other political prisoners has enraged public opinion here. Though President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has moved to discipline the army, the resurfacing of the case has also exposed other violations that may prove harder to address.
news.title: Exhuming a Political Killing Reopens Old Wounds in Brazil

news.abstract: Insurgents mount strikes on United States and Iraqi outposts across Iraq, using mortars and hidden roadside bombs to kill at least 18 Iraqi police officers and national guardsmen and wound dozens of Iraqis and Americans; American military official says attacks do not appear to be coordinated; Army of Ansar al-Sunna, militant Iraqi group that has taken credit for string of gruesome killings, posts video on Internet showing beheading of man they call 'crusader spy' for American forces; news agencies report that man claimed he sold drinks to American base in Mosul; flurry of violence underscores challenge facing American and Iraqi officials as planned national elections draw near; photo; map (M)
news.title: Rebel Attacks Kill 18 Iraqis; G.I.'s Injured
Dozens of Iraqi soldiers found shot to death

news.abstract: In a neighborhood here without lights, its pockmarked dirt streets and open sewers faintly visible under the full moon, the Dutch soldiers began a foot patrol on a recent evening. After getting out of their soft-top vehicles, the soldiers entered a street, wearing no helmets and pointing their guns down, chatting with Iraqis clustered in front of their homes.    ''Hello, Mister!'' some boys cried out, and they followed the soldiers to the bend in the road. Driving through the town later, the Dutch called out ''Salaam Aleikum'' to pedestrians. Many Iraqis, adults and children, waved at them.
news.title: Dutch Soldiers Find Smiles Are a More Effective Protection

news.abstract: In Judge Dursun Genel's snug little courtroom, the feuding couples shuttle in and out with stories of exhausted dreams and unhappy marriages.    ''We'll never have peace,'' a young woman recently told the judge, agreeing with her estranged husband that the only solution to their problems was divorce.
news.title: Turkey's Law Overhaul Overwhelms Courts and Citizens

news.abstract: Bunnatine H Greenhouse, chief contracting officer of Army Corps of Engineers, charges that Army gave Halliburton Co large contracts for work in Iraq and Balkans without following rules designed to ensure competition and fair prices to government; calls for high-level investigation of what she describes as threat to integrity of federal contracting program; says that after her repeated questions about Halliburton contracts, she was excluded from major decisions to award money and that her job status was threatened; Army refers Greenhouse's accusations to Pentagon's investigations bureau for review and promises to protect her position in meantime; photo (M)
news.title: Top Army Official Calls fora Halliburton Inquiry

news.title: New Guerrilla Factions Arise in Sudan Ahead of Peace Talks

news.abstract: Bush administration says it has concluded that some non-Iraqi prisoners captured by American forces in Iraq are not entitled to Geneva Conventions protections; this is important exception to public assertions by administration since Mar 2003; new opinion would essentially allow military and CIA to treat at least small number of non-Iraqi prisoners captured in Iraq in same way as members of Al Qaeda and Taliban captured in Afghanistan and elsewhere, for whom US has maintained that Geneva Conventions do not apply; at issue are CIA's secret transfers of dozen non-Iraqi prisoners for interrogation outside Iraq, and provision in conventions that bars such transfers; administration officials say new opinion represents consensus reached by lawyers from State Dept, Justice Dept, Pentagon, National Security Council and other agencies in discussions that began in Mar 2004 in response to opinion sought by CIA many months after it began transferring non-Iraqi prisoners beginning in Apr 2003 (M)
news.title: U.S. Action Bars Right of Some Captured in Iraq

news.abstract: Iraqi officials open investigation into role played by infiltrators in ambush that left 49 Iraqi National Guard trainees dead; there are growing indications that insurgents are being given inside information about movements of Iraqi security forces; United States military officials have long been skeptical of loyalty of Iraqi security forces, having seen some American-trained Iraqi soldiers take up arms against occupation forces during fighting in Apr; now even senior Iraqi government officials concede possibility that insurgents staged attack with help from members of Iraqi security forces; photo (M)
news.title: Inquiry Into Ambush Opens; Iraqi Forces Feared Infiltrated

news.abstract: The leader of Zimbabwe's political opposition, Morgan Tsvangirai, met with President Thabo Mbeki in Pretoria. It was Mr. Tsvangirai's first foreign trip since Zimbabwe officials seized his passport and charged him with treason 32 months ago; he was acquitted on Oct. 15. Mr. Mbeki has been working to open a dialogue between the opposition and President Robert Mugabe.   Michael Wines (NYT)

news.abstract: Japanese firefighters rescue boy, 2, from van buried by rock slide touched off by earthquake, Nagaoka; rescue is broadcast live, lifting nation's spirits after quake that left 33 dead, over 3,500 hurt and over 100,000 people living in shelters; others spend night in cars or garages, ready to flee new tremors; Japan, long accustomed to generously giving foreign aid, accepts emergency aid from South Korea and United States; boy's mother is pulled from wreakage, dead; his sister is also believed dead; map; photos (M)
news.title: Rescue of Toddler From Rubble 4 Days After Quake Lifts Japan's Spirit

news.abstract: Civilian, Yigit Alpogan, presides over Turkey's National Security Council for first time since 1980 military coup, reflecting quiet but major shift toward limiting military's political power; his appointment as secretary general followed constitutional amendments that cut number of posts reserved for military in council and several other government institutions; council has been army's vehicle for communicating its views on variety of issues (M)
news.title: Political Power of Turkish Army Seems to Fade

news.title: Warnings by Powell to Taiwan Provoke a Diplomatic Dispute

news.abstract: THE weekly zhikr ceremony organized by a brotherhood of Sufi Muslims noisily escalates toward its climax, with some 50 male participants in a double circle grunting God's name repeatedly at an ever faster pace while swinging rhythmically from side to side.    Julien Jalal Eddine Weiss loses himself in the choreographed prayers, rocking in a place of honor near a renowned Sufi troubadour wearing a large green turban and long white robe, plus several religious grandees wearing beanies and lengthy beards.
news.title: A Traveler Loses Himself in Middle Eastern Music

news.abstract: The Pentagon has ordered about 6,500 soldiers in Iraq to extend their tours, the first step the military has taken to increase its combat power there in preparation for the January elections, senior Defense Department officials said Friday.     About 3,500 members of the Second Brigade of the First Cavalry Division will stay in Iraq two months longer than initially ordered, and about 3,000 soldiers assigned to headquarters and support units of the First Infantry Division will have their tours extended by two and a half weeks.
news.title: Pentagon Extends Tours of Duty for About 6,500 U.S. Soldiers

news.abstract: More than a year and a half after hundreds of tons of explosives vanished at Al Qaqaa, the Iraqi weapons facility, the scene is a wasteland, ruled by mujahedeen. Page 12.
news.title: Eerie Scene at Iraqi Arms Site

news.abstract: When Kenyans go to the gas pump, they have several options -- regular, super, premium, diesel and, increasingly, a choice that has many local motorists scratching their heads, unleaded.    Lead-free gasoline may be the fuel of choice in most of the world but sub-Saharan Africa lags years behind when it comes to converting to cleaner-burning gasoline. On this continent, gas is sold at slick, modern stations and at roadside stands, where vendors use their mouths to help siphon fuel from plastic jugs. Many motorists mistakenly regard unleaded gas as suitable only for the latest model cars.
news.title: Belatedly, Africa Is Converting to Lead-Free Gasoline

news.abstract: Violent clashes between members of the Muslim Hui ethnic group and the majority Han group left nearly 150 people dead, journalists and witnesses in the region said today.
news.title: Ethnic Clashes Erupt in China, Leaving 150 Dead

news.abstract: A militant group claiming to have kidnapped three foreign election workers in Afghanistan told news agencies on Saturday that the hostages would be killed unless all Taliban prisoners in Afghanistan and in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, were released.    The group also called for international and Afghan forces hunting for the kidnappers to stop their pursuit, repeating a threat to kill the hostages if the pursuit continued.
news.title: Afghan Militants Repeat Threat to Kill 3

news.abstract: At 6:30 every morning in recent days, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, the leftist mayor of this giant city and arguably the most popular politician in the country, strides to a podium to face a gang of reporters. They are all bristling with questions about possible corruption in his government and a looming vote in Congress that could knock him off Mexico's presidential ballot in 2006.    A year ago, Mr. López, a populist with a history of organizing street protests to get his way, was considered by many pollsters as the most likely candidate to win the presidency in 2006 and the first candidate from the left-wing Democratic Revolutionary Party with a real chance of taking power.
news.title: Mexico City Mayor Faces Move to Lift His Immunity

news.abstract: Estimated 100,000 potential American voters live in Israel, many of them from critical swing states like Florida, Ohio, Michigan and Pennsylvania; estimated 10,000 Palestinian-Americans living in West Bank and Gaza Strip are eligible to vote; Republicans and Democrats are running voter registration campaigns, sometimes on Internet, hoping to capitalize on surge in voter interest this year; in last several presidential elections, Jewish voters in Israel favored Democratic candidate over Republican by 80 percent to 20 percent; Pres Bush is expected to make much stronger showing because of his support for Israel (M)
news.title: Both Parties Are Getting Out the U.S. Vote in Israel

news.abstract: Pakistan's leadership faces quandary over American-led antiterror effort; while army and government are enjoying fruits of billions of dollars in American aid, they are hunted by Islamic militants themselves; Pres Pervez Musharraf has narrowly escaped two assassination attempts; no one is quite sure what policies, if any, would end support for Islamic militancy in Pakistan, and there is fear that American policies are actually fueling that militancy; stalemate has emerged, with militants unable to carry out spectacular attacks, but government unable to eradicate militants (M)
news.title: Concern Rises in Pakistan of a War Without End

news.abstract: Allies of Venezuelan Pres Hugo Chavez expect to sweep crucial posts in nationwide regional elections on Oct 31; opposition is expected to lose as many as 100 mayoral posts, including one in Caracas, and as many as five governorships; opposition has been struggling to remain relevant since losing referendum to recall Chavez in Aug (M)
news.title: Sweep Expected in Venezuela Vote

news.abstract: Militants holding three foreign United Nations staff members in Afghanistan release videotape showing their hostages; say three will be killed if Muslim prisoners in Afghanistan and Guantanamo Bay are not released and foreign troops withdrawn from Afghanistan by Nov 3; video, broadcast by Al Jazeera, is strongest indication that Jaish-e-Muslimeen, breakaway group of Taliban, is adopting media-oriented tactics of kidnapping groups in Iraq; photo (M)
news.title: Afghan Militants Release Video of Hostages

news.abstract: Israeli cabinet and Palestinian officials hold separate gatherings dealing with same question: how to respond to absence of Yasir Arafat, who remains hospitalized in France with undiagnosed illness; Prime Min Ariel Sharon says Arafat's absence will not alter plans for unilateral Israeli withdrawal of soldiers and Jewish settlers from Gaza Strip next year; Sharon, who has refused to deal with Arafat, raises possibility that new Palestinian leadership could open door to negotiations envisioned under Middle East peace plan known as road map that collapsed shortly after it was introduced last year; Palestinian officials seek to demonstrate that Palestinian institutions are still working, but they do not want to give impression they are usurping power while Arafat is away; photos (M)
news.title: Arafat's Absence Raises Issue of How to Cope

news.abstract: Peter Hansen, United Nations refugee agency for Palestinians director, says Israel is trying to discredit agency work and requests apology for misleading statements, which could place agency workers at risk of increased hostility; UN Sec Gen Kofi Annan reiterates full support of Hansen's work (S)
news.title: World Briefing | United Nations: Refugee Chief Says Israel Incites Distrust
Euroskepticism fades in Polish countryside
Moves toward a more federal Europe may be out of step with voters' wishes : Despite EU victories, forces of disunity

news.abstract: Thousands of Uzbekistan citizens demonstrate in protest of new import laws in Kokand; authorities report that demonstration, which is rare in authoritarian Uzbekistan, was dispersed peacefully (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Asia: Uzbekistan: Several Thousand Protest

news.abstract: Heafily-armed Haitian gangs that had been united behind former president Jean-Bertrand Aristide have viciously turned against one another, catching tems of thousands of ordinary citizens in cross-fire; death toll in Port-au-Prince's poorest slum, Cite-Soleil, is impossible to know because police will not enter; photos; map (M)
news.title: Haiti's Political Vacuum Stokes Flames of Gang Violence

news.abstract: Retired Soviet physicist Leonid Grigorov hands over eight small containers of plutonium-238 to Altai regional authorities after learning of reward being offered for weapons; holds he found material in laboratory scrap heap in 1997 or 1998 and has kept it in his garage; type of plutonium could be used in making dirty-bomb (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Russia: A Pack Rat With Plutonium
Macedonian church guards its identity : Bishop's struggle reflects wider Balkan rift
Note links beheading to deaths of 84 Thais
Waiting, watching and losing sleep : On edge in Europe, too
Note calls beheading revenge for deaths of Muslim Thais
Bush wins 2nd term by a solid margin : Kerry failed to connect on economy

news.abstract: Pres Hamid Karzai is formally declared winner of Oct 9 presidential election by Afghanistan's electoral board after international panel announces that irregularities it found in voting would not change overall result; complaints of fraud by most of Karzai's 17 opponents detract from his victory as country's first directly elected head of state; his success is also overshadowed by kidnapping of three foreign United Nations election workers in Kabul last week by Jaish-e-Muslimeen, which threatens to kill them if its demands are not met (M)
news.title: Election of Karzai Is Declared Official

news.abstract: Charles Robert Jenkins, American Army sergeant who left his soldiers and walked into North Korea in 1965, receives light sentence after pleading guilty in court-martial held at Camp Zama in Japan; he is demoted to private, stripped of four decades of back pay and benefits, given dishonorable discharge and 30-day jail sentence; trial and sentencing seen relecting American political needs to mollify Japanese public opinion, which has been moved by drama of American defector and his Japanese wife, whom he met in North Korea after her abduction from Japan by North Korean agents; Jenkins apologizes to soldiers under his command, to Army and to United States; photo (M)
news.title: G.I. Deserter Tells of Cold, Hungry Times in North Korea

news.abstract: Iraq's interim prime minster appealed to what he called the "spectators" in the war in Iraq to become more involved.
news.title: Iraqi Leader Appeals to France and Germany for Aid
Former separatist leader sends a letter : A plea to Spain's rebels

news.abstract: Prime Min Ayad Allawi of Iraq, on trip to Europe, appeals to what he calls 'spectator' countries in war in Iraq--specifically France and Germany--to become more involved in creating peace and prosperity there; he is scheduled to meet in Brussels with French Pres Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Gerhard Schroder in what could be early test of any changing positions in Europe after Pres Bush's re-election; Allawi contends that even countries that opposed war are encouraged to build commercial relationship with Iraq based on reciprocal interests; in Rome, Allawi meets with Italian Prime Min Silvio Berlusconi, who repeats his pledge to keep 3,000 Italian troops deployed in Iraq; Allawi also meets with Pope John Paul II, who issues statement encouraging efforts of Iraqi people to establish democratic institutions; photo (M)
news.title: Iraqi Leader Asks Help of 'Spectator' Nations

news.abstract: Government planes in Ivory Coast conduct bombing raids against two rebel-held towns, ending tenuous yearlong cease-fire and signaling possible resumption of civil war; United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan calls airstrikes 'major violation' of cease-fire and warns Pres Laurent Gbagbo and rebels against further hostilities; 6,000 UN peacekeepers and 4,500 French troops are posted in Ivory Coast, charged with keeping warring parties at bay; map (M)
news.title: Ivory Coast Cease-Fire Ends With Airstrikes Against 2 Rebel Towns

news.abstract: The High Court ruled that a recount of the disputed presidential election last March had confirmed that President Chen Shui-bian won re-election. The court dismissed a Nationalist Party lawsuit contending that the election results should be overturned because of questions about a shooting incident in which the president was injured on the eve of the election -- an incident that may have elicited sympathy votes for him. Lien Chan, the defeated Nationalist candidate, vowed an appeal. Another Nationalist lawsuit, citing voting irregularities, is still pending.   Keith Bradsher (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Asia: Taiwan: Court Backs President

news.abstract: Election authorities said that the governor of Carabobo, a state that has been a bastion for anti-government forces, had lost his seat to a pro-government challenger in the regional elections on Sunday, cementing President Hugo Chávez's political dominance of the country. The victory by Luis Acosta, a former general, in the tight race against the incumbent, Henrique Salas, means that Mr. Chávez's allies swept nearly all the opposition candidates from important offices. Anti-government governors in six of eight states controlled by the opposition were voted out, leaving pro-Chávez allies in charge of 21 of Venezuela's 23 states. A pro-government mayor also took control of Caracas, which had been in opposition hands.   Juan Forero (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Americas: Venezuela: Chávez Allies Take 21 Of 23 States

news.abstract: Assembled leaders appeared to back away from proposed changes to resuscitate Europe's economy.
news.title: British and French Leaders Differ on Impact of Bush Victory for Europe

news.abstract: Carina Perelli, chief UN electoral expert, gives upbeat report on elections scheduled for Jan 2005 in Iraq; says that despite difficulties of working in such conflicted conditions, procedures are advancing on schedule (M)
news.title: U.N. Official Says Iraqi Vote Is Proceeding on Schedule

news.abstract: Wal-Mart discount store opens near Teotihuacan pyramids after months of protests; locals appear more interested in possible employment and better prices than preserving archaeological heritage of area around 1,800-year-old pyramids (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Americas: Mexico: Wal-Mart Opens Near Pyramids
Spanish honor author, but remain aloof : Like tilting at a windmill:Cervantes lost on Madrid

news.abstract: Leading Palestinian politicians are moving rapidly to prevent visible vacuum of power with Yasir Arafat apparently near death; are reaching out to disaffected younger legislators, Palestinian militant organizations and Israelis; photo (M)
news.title: Palestinian Politicians Try to Head Off a Power Struggle

news.abstract: Defense Department confirms deaths of two marines in Iraq
news.title: Names of the Dead

news.abstract: Defense Dept confirms death of one American soldier in Iraq, bringing total to 1,123
news.title: Names of the Dead

news.abstract: Yasir Arafat's deputy in the Palestine Liberation Organization, Mahmoud Abbas, and the Palestinian prime minister, Ahmed Qurie, will go to France on Monday.
news.title: Palestinian Leaders to Visit Arafat's Doctors

news.abstract: Palestinian law, in event Yasir Arafat cannot serve because of death or illness, calls for speaker of parliament to become caretaker leader of Palestinian Authority until elections, which must be held within two months; obstacles to elections may cause Palestinian Authority to ignore law and simply appoint successor, who is likely to be Mahmoud Abbas; another possibility is collective leadership, with elections postponed; municipal elections are scheduled for December (M)
news.title: Palestinian Line of Succession Answers and Raises Questions

news.abstract: Constitution signed by European Union leaders makes no mention of Europe's Christian roots; strong secularism has dominated European political discourse for decades, but now rare debate has opened over social issues as many conservative critics charge that secularism is getting out of hand (M)
news.title: Europe, Seeking Political Unity, Stumbles Over Issue of Religion

news.abstract: Negotiations with officials from the Afghan government and the United Nations ended without result.
news.title: Afghan Militants Hold Talks on Hostages, but No Deal Yet

news.abstract: Explosions and heavy gunfire thunder across Falluja as American troops seize control of two strategic bridges, hospital and other objectives in first stage of long-expected invasion of city, center of Iraqi insurgency; Prime Min Ayad Allawi proclaims state of emergency for 60 days, which gives him broad powers to impose curfews, order house-to-house searches and detain suspects; force is composed of between 10,000 and 15,000 American soldiers and marines backed by newly trained Iraqi forces; American commanders brace troops for brutal block-by-block battle to take control and capture, kill or disperse estimated 3,000 to 4,000 insurgents; most civilians in Falluja, city of about 250,000, are believed to have left; Defense Sec Donald Rumsfeld and Gen Richard Myers are monitoring combat preparation and updated combat reports; photos; maps (M)
news.title: G.I.'s Open Attack to Take Falluja From Iraq Rebels

news.abstract: French Defense Min Michele Alliot-Marie announces deployment of additional 600 troops to Ivory Coast after loyalist citizens rebel in streets of Abidjan and attack French citizens and French-owned businesses; Pres Lauren Gbagbo says he ordered army offensive in north halted and urges demonstrators to stop violent protests and attacks; United Nations Security Council is meeting to discuss possible penalties against government for breaking cease-fire and allowing violence; loyalists accuse French of aiding rebel insurgency (M)
news.title: More French Troops Are Sent to Ivory Coast as Violence Flares
Paris tries to rein in Ivory Coast

news.abstract: Many young people have quit eastern Germany to escape the high unemployment, running at over 18 percent.
news.title: East Germans Ambivalent 15 Years After Fall of Berlin Wall

news.abstract: Jaish-e-Muslimeen, Taliban splinter group holding United Nations workers hostage in Afghanistan, send spokesman to negotiate with Afghan officials and United Nations representatives in southern Afghanistan; hand over list of 25 prisoners whom they want released; hostages, who were kidnapped on Oct 28, are British-Irish woman Annetta Flanigan, Kosovo Albanian woman Shqipe Habibi and Filipino Angelito Nayan; negotiations to secure release of captives have not been successful (S)
news.title: Afghan Militants Conduct Talks Over 3 Hostages

news.abstract: Seven people returning home after Nocupetaro religious festival are gunned down by assassins apparently mistaking them for someone else; three children, 5-year-old Guadalupe Hernandez and 14-year-olds Armando Hernandez and Maria Hernandez Figueroa, and four adults are killed; Michoacan State Attorney General Miguel Angel Arellano Pulido reports that two local police officers have been taken into custody for involvement in shooting (S)
news.title: 7 in Family Slain in Mexico in Mix-Up Laid to Police Renegades

news.abstract: Left-wing Sandinista Party gains influence in country after weekend municipal elections; party now controls 15 of 17 provincial capitals, including Managua; Pres Enrique Bolanos party appears to be losing support amid allegations that leader accepted illegal campaign contributions (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Americas: Nicaragua: Sandinistas' Strong Showing
A membership issue:billions in purchases : Turkey's economic attraction to EU

news.abstract: Indonesian government panel presents report on water quality in Buyat Bay, which residents and some environmental experts hold has been toxically polluted by Newmont Mining Corporation, world's biggest gold producer; report holds that although mine waste deposited is polluted with significant levels of arsenic and mercury, water quality meets Indonesian standards; villagers, who have filed $543 million lawsuit against Newmont, contend that they suffer waste related health problems as direct result of bay contamination; Dave A Baker, Newmont vice pres for environment affairs, says that mine is not causing harm to environment, but has shut down operation there; levels of contaminates debated; Indonesian journalist suggests Newmont tried to bribe reporters at news conference on recent findings after envelope of money was found in press kit; Newmont holds money was travel reimbursement; map; drawing; photo (L)
news.title: Report Heightens Pollution Dispute at Indonesian Bay

news.abstract: Diana, Princess of Wales Memorial Fountain, which was designed by American landscape architect Kathryn Gustafson and opened in July in Hyde Park, London, has been plagued with problems; $6.7 million Mobius strip carved of Welsh granite requires constant patrolling by brigade of guards, who are busy enforcing rules and straining leaves and sticks from water; Parks Department holds that fountain and surroundings are not ready for thousands of visitors, but many people are critical of design; fountain has been closed several times and changes continue to be made to improve function and safety; photo (M)
news.title: Diana's Park Memorial Today: A Font of Faultfinding

news.abstract: United States Defense Department confirms deaths of four American service members who died in Iraq (S)
news.title: Names of the Dead

news.abstract: Two separate bombs thought to be set by Maoist rebels injure 39 people in Katmandu and Bhaktapur, Nepal; security analysts hold attacks are meant to show that recent arrest of Maoist leader Comrade Prachanda by government forces has not had effect on insurgency (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Asia: Nepal: Katmandu Bomb Injures 37

news.abstract: Amsterdam funeral for Dutch filmmaker Theo van Gogh, who was killed last week by Muslim extremist, polarizes national debate over conservative Islam in nation that is traditionally tolerant; public anger has risen since killing and several retaliatory actions by both Muslims and opponents to Islam have taken place, including bombing of Eindhoven Muslim elementary school, suspicious fire at Uden elementary school and attempts to burn down Protestant churches in Rotterdam, Utrecht and Amersfoort; anti-immigration movement, which began in 2001 and was spearheaded by Pim Fortuyn, who was killed by activist in 2002, has grown in force and may inhibit discussion about political change and religious freedoms; van Gogh's killing is, at least for now, roadblock to discussion on national unity; photos (L)
news.title: In Mourning Slain Filmmaker, Dutch Confront Limitations of Their Tolerance

news.abstract: United States Sec of State Colin L Powell, speaking at news conference during visit with Mexican Foreign Minister Luis Ernesto Derbez, assures Mexican officials that Pres George W Bush is committed to pursuing temporary worker program in US; admits, however, that plan, which gives temporary resident status to some illegal aliens holding jobs in US, will need support of Congress to become law (S)
news.title: Powell, in Mexico, Pledges Migrant Reform

news.abstract: Iraqi Islamic Party, Iraq's most prominent Sunni political party, withdraws from interim government after United States and Iraqi forces invade Falluja; leading Sunni clerics also call for boycott of national elections scheduled for Jan 2005; boycott of Sunnis, who make up 20 percent of population, could undermine legitimacy of election and new government; although many Sunni leaders would have preferred Falluja be secured through peaceful negotiations, prominent Sunni politician Hajim Al Hassani admits no one has come up with non-violent solution to overcome insurgency in Falluja and ensure safety of region; political fallout from attack on Falluja is uncertain as battle there continues; photo (M)
news.title: Sunni Party Leaves Iraqi Government Over Falluja Attack

news.abstract: Bosnian Serb authorities issue, for first time, official apology for 1995 Srebrenica massacre of estimated 8,000 Muslim men and boys; statement comes after intense international pressure to accept responsibility for incident and renew efforts to bring those involved to trial (S)
news.title: Bosnian Serbs Apologize for Srebrenica Massacre

news.abstract: Palestinian nationalist, guerrilla leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Yasir Arafat dies at age 75; was divisive figure central to peace talks and violence with Israel over Palestinian state; oversaw Palestinian Liberation Organization, which pursued sovereignty and independence, often violently; photos (L)
news.title: Yasir Arafat, Father and Leader of Palestinian Nationalism, Dies at 75

news.abstract: Dublin hospital confirms first indigenous case of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, incurable and degenerative brain disorder that is caused by eating meat infected with Mad Cow disease, in Ireland (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Ireland: Rare Brain Disease Confirmed

news.abstract: Documents released by Rep Henry A Waxman, Democrat and House Committee on Government Reform ranking minority member, show that American diplomats pressured Halliburton Company to keep using Altanmia, Kuwaiti subcontractor, despite unusually high prices for oil delivery services; Altanmia was hired by Halliburton subsidiary Kellogg Brown & Root, and prices for service were immediately questioned by critics in Congress, but defended by Halliburton; Pentagon is still considering possible call for refund and FBI is examing fuel transactions; some documents suggest American diplomats were eager to gain Kuwait's wider cooperation and provide greater fuel supplies to Iraq and in doing so rejected questions about Altanmia pricing (M)
news.title: Halliburton May Have Been Pressured by U.S. Diplomats to Disregard High Fuel Prices

news.abstract: From the Vatican to the Palestinian refugee camps of Jordan, tributes poured in today for Yasir Arafat, a man regarded as an international leader by many and a terrorist by others.
news.title: Tributes for Arafat Focus on Efforts for Palestinian State

news.abstract: Two Dutch-American brothers, who converted to Islam are among seven people arrested in antiterrorism raid in Netherlands; raid is part of continuing investigation into Islamic terrorist network linked with extremists in Morocco and Spain (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: The Netherlands: Report Says 2 Terror Suspects Are Dutch-Americans

news.abstract: Military judge orders trials of soldiers accused of abuse at Iraq's Abu Ghraib prison to be moved to Fort Hood, Tex, from Baghdad; seven reservist soldiers from 372nd military police company based in Cresaptown, Maryland, stand accused of abuse (M)
news.title: Trials of G.I.'s at Abu Ghraib to Be Moved to the U.S.

news.abstract: Lamborghini spokesman Sergio Fontana discusses company's decision to donate Lamborghini Gallardo to Italian highway police to commemorate 152nd anniversary of national police force; Chief Inspector Laura Ciano and Superintendent Vincenzo Bizzarro, who have been trained to drive car, describe car's special features and experiences driving eye-catching police vehicle; Italy has road fatality rate higher than European average; officials admit speeders who are stopped by Gallardo are less angry when they receive ticket; photos (M)
news.title: Whoosh! For Speeders, Speedier Justice, via Lamborghini
A grim report on future grabs Europe's attention

news.abstract: World Health Organization takes first step toward approval of smallpox research that would involve gene manipulation; group advisory committee recommends that Russian and American high biosecurity labs perform research in hopes of finding drugs to treat disease; smallpox was eradicated in 1980, but concerns have grown that smallpox could become bioterrorism threat; so far, only drug cidofovir is candidate for treating smallpox; proposed study would involve insertion of green fluorescent market protein, gene, into variola virus (S)
news.title: W.H.O. Panel Backs Gene Manipulation in Smallpox Virus

news.abstract: Defense Department confirms deaths of 16 US servicemen in Iraq
news.title: Names of the Dead

news.abstract: Dutch police raid terrorist training camp for Kurdish separatists in Liempde; arrest 38 people there and at other places in country in ongoing crackdown on militants; are looking for Abu Khaled, Syrian who they say is leader of Islamic cell responsible for killing Dutch filmmaker Theo van Gogh; map (M)
news.title: Dutch Hold 38 on Terror Charges After Raid on Camp

news.abstract: Yasir Arafat is buried in Ramallah, West Bank, in extraordinary scene of grief and chaos; thousands of Palestinians climb walls of his compound and surge around his coffin, trying to bear it aloft; Palestinian security guards are unable to hold back frenzied flow of some 20,000 mourners; passionate scene is in contrast to Arafat's Cairo funeral service earlier in day, which was restricted to officials and Arafat's wife Suha and daughter Zahwa, 9; photos (M)
news.title: Arafat Is Buried in Chaotic Scene in the West Bank

news.abstract: Mullah Mohammad Omar, deposed Taliban leader who is thought to be living in Pakistan and overseeing resistance movement, vows to take back control of Afghanistan (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Asia: Afghanistan: Taliban Leader Vows Return
Globalist : The real cost of gold is far away, deep down

news.abstract: Defense Dept confirms death of three American marines in Iraq, bringing total to 1,166
news.title: Names of the Dead

news.abstract: Artemisinin, extract of sweet wormwood, is most cost-effective malaria treatment available, but shortages loom in 40 tropical countries that have made it centerpiece of their antimalarial efforts amid soaring demand and rising prices; plant is cultivated almost exclusively in China and Vietnam; multidrug combinations including artemisinin cost 10 to 20 times more than older malaria drugs but are more effective; Novartis's announcement that it will fall short on supply promised to World Health Organization provides most vivid evidence of problem; photo (M)
news.title: Plant Shortage Leaves Campaigns Against Malaria at Risk

news.abstract: Meanwhile, Mahmoud Abbas escaped injury as Palestinians waged a deadly gun battle during a mourning service for Yasir Arafat today.
news.title: Palestinians Schedule Election for Jan. 9

news.abstract: Interim Iraqi Prime Min Ayad Allawi may have jeopardized political future by ordering attack on Falluja; both Sunnis and Shiites have condemned attack; militants kidnapped Alawi's cousin and his family on Nov 9, threatening to kill them if attack is not halted; Allawi is said to have insisted attack begin by Nov 12 so that there will be enough time to wrap it up by Nov 22, when he will attend conference in Egypt on Iraq's future (M)
news.title: For Iraqi Leader, Political Risks of Attack on Falluja Grow

news.abstract: Army tanks and fighting vehicles blast their way into last main rebel stronghold in Falluja at sundown after American warplanes and artillery prepare way with savage barrage on district; as battle intensifies in Falluja, insurgents roam streets of important northern city of Mosul and nearby town of Ramadi; photos (M)
news.title: U.S. Armored Forces Blast Their Way Into Rebel Nest in Falluja

news.abstract: Izhavto automobile company in Izhevsk, Russia, is struggling to adapt to life under capitalism, and to laws of supply and demand; it recently shut down its plant and laid off 12,500 workers after running out of places to put its new cars, which it kept producing even as sales declined; map; graph (M)
news.title: Workers Feel the Growing Pains of Russia's Auto Industry

news.abstract: Pitched battles erupt between insurgents and American and Iraqi forces in northern city of Mosul; carloads of insurgents drive unhindered through parts of city and attack security forces; hundreds of policemen in Mosul flee when attackers storm at least six police stations, taking American military by surprise; fighters barricade themselves in police station, wounding at least 20 Iraqi security commandos; thousands of Kurdish militiamen from outside Mosul begin taking up positions in streets; maps; caht (M)
news.title: Raids in the Mosul Region Undermine Value of Victories

news.abstract: Virtually every house that marine company goes through in Shuhada neighborhood of Falluja, considered final redoubt for insurgents, contains weapons, as well as booby traps and time bombs; they also find lists of names, as well as photographs and maps; map (M)
news.title: What the Rebels Left Behind: Arms, Grime, Death Lists
Extremist parties unite for '06 ticket : The far right knocks at Bundestag's door

news.abstract: Army Corps of Engineers is trying to demote Bunnatine H Greenhouse, its contracting director who has criticized corps for turning too readily and too generously to Halliburton Co for urgent repair of Iraqi oil fields; Greenhouse is determined to stay despite sarcastic remarks of her superiors about whistle-blowers; photo (M)
news.title: A Watchdog Follows the Money in Iraq

news.abstract: Louise Arbour said today that she was concerned that the rules of war intended to protect civilians and combatants had been violated.
news.title: U.N. Chief for Human Rights Raises Concern on Falluja
Germany's far right knocks at Bundestag's door

news.abstract: By time-hallowed tradition, the English pub evokes an image of low beams, warm ales and the toxic swirling smog of tobacco smoke. But not, perhaps, for much longer.
news.title: Blair Sees England's Pubs as a Smoke-Free Zone

news.abstract: Russian Pres Vladimir V Putin plays down comments by Foreign Min Sergey V Lavrov that suggest Russia would give two of southernmost Kurile Islands to Japan; islands were seized by Russia at end of World War II and have been impediment to improved relations between nations (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Asia: Putin Indicates Kurile Deal Is Not Likely Soon

news.abstract: Serbian Pres Svetozar Marovic welcomes Croatian Prime Min Ivo Sanader for first official visit by Croatian prime min since before 1990's war between nations; photo (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Serbia: Croatian Premier In First Visit
Globalist : South Africa's ghosts haunt thinking on HIV

news.abstract: Hamas and Islamic Jihad say they will not take part in Palestinian presidential election set for January, and Hamas says it will not suspend attacks against Israel; Prime Min Ariel Sharon indicates that if new Palestinian leadership cracks down on violence he would work on coordinating Gaza withdrawal plan; new PLO leader Mahmoud Abbas holds talks with Hamas leaders in Gaza (M)
news.title: Palestinians Face Boycotts of Election for President

news.abstract: US in days before Falluja invasion dropped more than million leaflets urging insurgents not to fight and Iraqi police in streets gave out leaflets with lurid images warning that insurgents twist minds of Iraqi youth; photo; insurgents offered own propaganda, such as poster showing Statue of Liberty being pulled down; US military teams now clearing city will continue 'soft war' of promoting Iraqi security forces and government and publicizing reconstruction (M)
news.title: Sides in Falluja Fight for Hearts and Minds

news.abstract: Iranian opposition group says it has new evidence that Iran is producing enriched uranium at covert facility in Tehran that has not been disclosed to UN inspectors (S)
news.title: Group Says Iran Has Secret Nuclear Arms Program

news.abstract: US military races to contain spreading insurgency, sending hundreds of soldiers and armored vehicles into Mosul to root out bands of rebels who commandeered parts of city as Americans battled their way into Falluja; family of kidnapped aid worker Margaret Hassan believes she is woman shown being executed on videotape released by insurgents; photos; map; US military investigates videotaped fatal shooting of apparently wounded insurgent by marine in Falluja mosque; snipers continue shooting at troops roaming debris-covered streets on Falluja as residents emerge warily; rebels continue wave of attacks across Sunni Triangle, in Baquba and Ramadi, and bomb oil pipelines near Kirkuk; US soldiers is killed and another wounded by bomb near Baghdad (M)
news.title: U.S. Troops Move to Drive Out Rebels in North of Iraq

news.abstract: Indian Prime Min Manmohan Singh, visiting Kashmir, offers unconditional talks with anyone willing to renounce violence and $5.3 billion economic package intended to 'win hearts and minds' of residents; plans to create 24,000 government jobs; visit comes as unspecified number of troops begin withdrawing from area in India's first declared force cut since anti-Indian insurgency began in 1989; Singh suggests there can be further troop cuts if situation approves and infiltration of militants declines; violence continues, with security forces killing two militants under mile from Singh's public meeting site; map (M)
news.title: India's Offer for Peace Talks on Kashmir Is Sweetened With Aid

news.abstract: Portraits of leader Kim Jong Il reportedly have been removed from honored spots in North Korea and official news outlets are dropping honorific 'Dear Leader;' regional analysts debate whether he loses grip in power or, more likely, orchestrates downsizing of own personality cult (M)
news.title: Monitors of North Korean News Note Dip in Reverence for Kim
With purges in Myanmar, reform outlook dims

news.abstract: French Pres Jacques Chirac says American-led invasion of Iraq has made world more dangerous, spurring Islamic terrorism around world, although Saddam Hussein's departure was positive to certain extent, British television interview; shows disdain for Bush administration and dismisses Prime Min Tony Blair's unyielding support for Bush, interview in British newspapers; photo (M)
news.title: Chirac Says War in Iraq Spreads Terrorism
Growing importance of EU is lure : Lobbyists beat a path to power in Brussels

news.abstract: Most popular Palestinian candidate for new leadership is Marwan Barghouti, who is considering run for presidency of Palestinian Authority from Israeli jail cell where he is serving five life terms on terrorism conviction; photos; Barghouti, 45, speaks Hebrew and English and has sophisticated understanding of Israelis, both from stints in prison and from formerly close ties to Israeli politicians; Israeli remember him for support of two-state solution and speculation abounds that he could be released now, but that is considered unlikely because court found he has blood on his hands from attacks of recent years; Barghouti is leader in rising generation of Palestinians who grew up under Israeli occupation and came to admire aspects of Israeli democracy; his wife Fadwa, 40-year-old lawyer, voices commonplace complaints about corruption under Yasir Arafat (M)
news.title: Jailed in Israel, Palestinian Symbol Eyes Top Post

news.abstract: London court hearing Elaine Day's suit over dismissal from Prince Charles's household staff hears memo that prince wrote in 2002 complaining about people who think they are 'qualified to do things far above their capabilities' and blaming 'learning culture' in schools that admits no failure by anyone; not clear is how former secretary got memo or whether it referred to her; photo; education official calls prince old-fashioned, but royal spokesman says Charles means that people have different talents to be developed (M)
news.title: Prince Charles Says He Knows His Place and Yours, Too

news.abstract: UN Security Council convenes unusual session in Kenya to try to bring peace to neighboring Sudan; members agree on resolution that will suggest unspecified action against parties that do not cease hostilities in Darfur (S)
news.title: U.N. Council, in Nairobi, Again Warns Sudan
Letter from America : Fear factor:Did Bush use it better than Kerry?

news.abstract: European Union Parliament approves new executive branch to be led by incoming commissioner Jose Manuel Durao Barroso of Portugal (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: New European Commissioners

news.abstract: Fred Eckhard, United Nations Sec Gen Kofi Annan's spokesman, reports that there is clear evidence that some UN peacekeepers in Congo have committed acts of sexual abuse against women and children; team of investigators is being sent immediately; 70 complaints have been made and around 20 are actionable (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Africa: Congo: Annan Says Peacekeepers Abused Women And Children
Myanmar junta freeing some of its foes

news.abstract: US, faced with polarizing division in General Assembly, abandons its attempt to obtain UN treaty banning human cloning, including that done in name of medical research; outcome--agreement to come up with nonbinding declaration against cloning to reproduce humans--falls far short of US goal and represents setback for Pres Bush (M)
news.title: U.S. Drops Effort for Treaty Banning Cloning
Italians rally to keep Fiat 500 on the road

news.abstract: US and Iraqi troops raid Abu Hanifa Mosque in Baghdad, killing at least three Iraqis; Iraqi commanders in Mosul stage numerous raids in search of rebel hideouts as up to dozen decapitated bodies are found strewn about city; map; photo (M)
news.title: G.I.'s and Iraqis Raid Mosque, Killing 3

news.abstract: Pres Bush, on first day of meeting of Pacific Rim leaders in Santiago, Chile, steps up pressure on Iran over nuclear weapons production even as he tries to establish unified front against nuclear challenge from North Korea; meets with leaders of China, Japan and South Korea, urging each to draw North Korea back into six-nation negotiations; issues direct challenge to Kim Jong Il to get rid of his weapons program; calls indications that Iran is accelerating its uranium enrichment program 'a very serious matter' that undercuts Iran's denials that it is seeking to build weapons; photo (M)
news.title: Bush Says Iran Speeds Output of A-Bomb Fuel

news.abstract: After two years at Slobodan Milosevic's trial in The Hague in which the prosecution and its witnesses presented him variously as a brutal dictator and a war criminal, he is now hearing sweeter words from witnesses.     The defense for Mr. Milosevic, the former Yugoslav president and Serbian leader, has been repeatedly disrupted since it began in July, both by his health problems and legal wrangling, and has only recently resumed. In November, he won an appeal, regaining the right to lead his own defense after many of his witnesses refused to cooperate with court-appointed lawyers. news.abstract: In a rare show of unity, Turkey's president, prime minister, army chief and opposition party leader issued a strong joint protest against European Union moves to impose new conditions for the start of membership talks. They were reacting to the latest draft statement, prepared for the European leaders' Dec. 17 summit meeting in Brussels, which reportedly criticizes Turkey's record on torture and would set tougher standards for its entry to the European bloc than for other countries. France, Austria and the Netherlands, among others, have resisted issuing Turkey an invitation to begin negotiations. Their hesitation has fueled anger across Turkey, and the Turkish leaders, clearly irritated, suggested that the Europeans were treating them unfairly.   Susan Sachs (NYT)

news.abstract: After a three-hour firefight here in northern Iraq this month, American commanders were surprised to learn that one of the 22 insurgents they had killed was a Saudi. Even more intriguing, one of the principal leaders of the insurgency attended the funeral, the commanders learned.     This was Mohammed Sharkawa, who is described as a former member of the Ansar al-Sunna organization who now directs several hundred insurgents here in Mosul. As one commander, who said Mr. Sharkawa had killed several of his own cousins, put it, he is ''a brutally ruthless criminal, almost like a mob wiseguy who started whacking dudes.''

news.abstract: Two weeks of negotiations at a United Nations conference here on climate change ended early Saturday with a weak pledge to start limited, informal talks on ways to slow down global warming, after the United States blocked efforts to begin more substantive discussions.    The main focus was to discuss the Kyoto Protocol on global warming, which goes into force on Feb. 16 and will require industrial nations to make substantial cuts in their emissions of so-called greenhouse gases. But another goal had been to draw the United States, which withdrew from the accord in 2001, back into discussions about ways to mitigate climate change after 2012, when the Kyoto agreement expires.
news.title: U.S. Waters Down Global Commitment to Curb Greenhouse Gases

news.abstract: Gen. Augusto Pinochet, under investigation on corruption charges and increasingly feeble, is not much of a factor in Chilean politics these days. But it is only now, nearly 15 years after he was forced to leave power, that the authoritarian governing structure he left behind to hamstring his civilian successors is being dismantled.    Thanks to an agreement between the Socialist-led coalition now in office and the right-wing opposition, Chile's Congress is set to approve a constitutional reform plan that will expand civilian authority and reduce the military's ability to interfere in governing the country. The package also restores the president's power to fire military commanders and eliminates appointive Senate seats for former commanders.
news.title: 15 Years After Pinochet, Chile Begins to Dismantle His Rule

news.abstract: A week after the Supreme Court gave the government the constitutional go-ahead to expand marriage rights to gays and lesbians, a bitter battle has emerged in Parliament that is creating deep fissures in the Liberal and Conservative parties.    Polls indicate that a comfortable majority of Canadians actively support or passively accept legislation being prepared by Prime Minister Paul Martin to redefine marriage across the country. Already courts in six provinces and one territory, all told including 85 percent of the population of nearly 32 million, have struck down old marriage laws to allow gays and lesbians to marry. Only minor protests have occurred.

news.abstract: An Ontario government report recommended that Muslims be allowed to use religious laws to settle inheritance and family disputes outside the court system. The report came after an Islamic group, the Canadian Society of Muslims, announced plans to apply Shariah, a legal code based on the Koran, to settle disputes over issues like marriage, divorce and property. The report's recommendation drew sharp criticism from several groups, including the Canadian Council of Muslim Women, which said Shariah contradicts Canadian laws of equality for women. Provincial law already gives religious authorities limited powers to arbitrate civil matters, but plans to extend those rights to include Shariah have stirred bitter debate. The report, prepared by Marion Boyd, a former Ontario attorney general and a feminist activist, also recommends safeguards to ensure that neither party in a Shariah arbitration is subject to domestic violence and that there be ample opportunities to appeal decisions.   Colin Campbell (NYT)

news.abstract: The authorities have arrested more than 10 men over the past nine months on charges of spying on the country's nuclear activities for the United States and Israel, Intelligence Minister Ali Yunesi told IRNA news agency. Mr. Yunesi said that an opposition group based in Iraq, the People's Mujahedeen, had played a central role in the espionage. In 2002, the organization's military wing, the National Council of Resistance, revealed the existence of a secret nuclear facility in Natanz and a heavy-water complex near Arak. news.abstract: Experts at Pacific Tsunami Warning Center in Honolulu had no way of knowing that earthquake that struck off Indonesia had generated devastating tsunami and no way to warn people most likely to suffer; sequence of events as knowledge of earthquake, tsunami and destruction unfolded suggest speed and precision of science and modern communication, as well as their limits; scientists do not have tools to tell when earthquake has created one; for Pacific Ocean, there are computer models to analyze consequences of earthquake, based on years of observations of previous quakes and tsunamis; for Indian Ocean, where tsunamis are rare, there are no such models (M)
news.title: At Warning Center, Alert for the Quake, None for a Tsunami

news.abstract: Viktor A Yushchenko, opposition leader, is Ukraine's presumptive president-elect after virtually all votes are counted; leads Prime Min Viktor F Yanukovich by 52 percent to 44 percent; Yanukovich refuses to accept results and says he will challenge them in court, but he has mustered few supporters; Kiev is calm after weeks of civil disobedience, and there are signs that evident outcome of election is being recognized abroad; Secretary of State Colin L Powell says election appears free and fair; Foreign Ministry of Belarus, Ukraine's neighbor, says it respects decision of Ukrainian people; European Union foreign policy chief Javier Solana also signals his satisfaction; importantly, leaders of prominent team of international election observers declare conduct of voting was substantial improvement over previous rounds; photo (M)
news.title: Yushchenko Wins 52% of Vote; Rival Vows a Challenge

news.abstract: Peace talks began near the Uganda-Sudan border between the Ugandan government and an elusive rebel group called the Lord's Resistance Army, which has terrorized Ugandans for the last 18 years. The rebels, led by a mystic named Joseph Kony, have reinforced their ranks over the years by kidnapping children. The group's spokesman, Sam Kolo, told the government officials and journalists present: ''We could kill you all now for nothing but that's not our aim. We are committed to peace 100 percent.''   Marc Lacey (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Africa: Uganda: Government And Rebels In Talks

news.abstract: World Health Orgn officials say large quantities of clean water would be best medicine for tens of thousands of tsunami survivors at risk from diseases spread by dirty water, mosquitoes and crowding; say water shortages have already occurred in Maldives and Sri Lanka, and tanker trucks are needed to provide clean water; water-purifying tablets are being rushed into affected countries, along with medicines to treat dehydration that can result from diarrhea; photo (M)

news.abstract: Kurdish leaders are determined to preserve informal but unmistakable autonomy they now enjoy in Erbil and entire Kurdish region of northern Iraq; residents already call area Kurdistan; territory is world apart from Iraq, with building boom, new apartments, hospitals and shopping centers; Kurdish sector is calm, free of violence plaguing large areas of Iraq; tight security is maintained by swarms of Kurdish police officers and militiamen; some Iraqi leaders resent most important safeguard of Kurdish independence: power to veto new constitution; photos; map (M)
news.title: Iraq's Kurds Enjoy Self-Rule and Are Trying to Keep It

news.abstract: Abdul Hamid Ansar woke up before dawn Thursday, whispered prayers, gulped down a cup of steaming tea and resumed his surreal new existence: overseer of Sri Lanka's coast of death.     Mr. Ansar, a shy, 42-year-old divisional secretary, the Sri Lankan equivalent of an American city manager, has led the search for bodies along a four-mile stretch of congested coastline where 9,000 people are believed to have been killed when a tsunami crashed in on Sunday. His small slice of Sri Lanka appears to have the highest death toll of any single community in Asia outside of Aceh Province in Indonesia.
news.title: In a Corner of Sri Lanka, Devastation and Divisions

news.abstract: Human tally in Indonesia jumps to 80,000 after officials report uncovering 28,000 more bodies in Aceh Province, near epicenter of enormous undersea earthquake; food drops and other aid trickles toward region from around world, but injured and stranded in many places still have to fend for themselves; death toll in all affected countries surges past 120,000, and international health experts say at least three times that number may be seriously injured, their survival dependent on arrival of urgent medical aid; Secretary General Kofi Annan says World Bank pledged $250 million, raising total amount devoted to emergency to nearly $500 million; says more than 30 countries and millions of individuals have joined in global campaign; says World Bank, along with United States, Australia, India and Japan have formed 'core group' to lead coordinating relief drive; extent of red tape is demonstrated when United Nations Children's Fund plane with enough aid to help 200,000 people lands at Jakarta airport, and is forced to wait day for customs clearance before it could be moved to disaster scene far north; fears of looting and disease rise, and people throughout region remain jittery; Indian officials issue warning of another tsunami, sending people in India and Sri Lanka fleeing from beaches; warning appears to be false alarm; photos; map (L)
news.title: Many Still in Need as Aid Is Trickling to Stricken Area

news.abstract: Experts say thousands of deaths might have been avoided if warning systems had been in place to alert people around rim of Indian Ocean of tsunami; no such system exists there now; those who design and use wireless technology known as Short Message Service, currently used for chatter and advertisements, say it could be used to jumpstart governments' warning networks; text messaging is wildly popular worldwide and has accompanied international boom in cellphone use (M)
news.title: Text Messaging Pushed for Use as Disaster Warning Systems
